text: This is it — the mini capstone, where everything from Chapters 6 through 8 comes together into one real, complete pipeline. No new concepts today, just assembling the ones you already have into something that actually answers a question.

Before any code: which pickup zones have the highest average fare, and how many trips come from each? A real data engineering task starts with a business question, not 'write some PySpark' — and writing that question down gives you a way to check, at the end, whether the pipeline actually did its job.

Extract is its own function, with logging wrapped around it — Lesson 39's pattern. When this runs unattended later, the log tells you exactly how many trip rows and zone rows came in, which is the first thing you'd check if the final numbers ever looked wrong.

Real trip records include fares of zero or less, zero-distance trips, and occasional missing fields — none of which belong in an average fare calculation. The clean function filters those out and logs the before and after row counts, so the effect is visible, not just silently trusted.

Transform joins trips to the zone lookup table so a numeric location ID becomes a real place name — and now with a validation check built in: if any trips come back with no matching zone, that's logged as a warning. Aggregate then answers the actual question, with one judgment call: ignoring zones with fewer than 50 trips, so one lucky expensive fare in a tiny zone can't fake its way to the top.

Load writes the result to disk, and run_pipeline chains all five steps together: extract, clean, transform, aggregate, load. Splitting it into small, named functions mirrors Chapter 6's ETL design exactly, and it's what makes it possible to check each piece on its own instead of untangling one giant script.

Once you can explain why filtering out low-trip zones matters before trusting a fare ranking, and why splitting the pipeline into small functions matters, you're ready for Lesson 48 — where we prove this pipeline's output is actually correct, not just error-free.
